newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's says working to prevent another spiral.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's says working to prevent another spiral.

text.p: Lloyd's of London is working to prevent the development of the kind of reinsurance spiral that led to massive losses in the late 1980s and early 1990s, according to the markets director of regulation David Gittings.
Commenting in the society's newsletter Limelight, Gittings said close and regular monitoring of underwriting transactions now carried out would provide early warning of undue concentrations of risk.
"I would add that we have no evidence to substantiate the re-emergence of a spiral to date," said Gittings.
Last month members' agent Christie Brockbank Shipton Ltd (CBSL) warned that the signs indicated a spiral could reoccur.

Spiral occurs when syndicates reinsure some or part of risks they have already insured. This reduces the amount of premium income available to pay any claims as more of the premium is taken out in brokerage and other fees.
Such concentration of risk caused massive losses for the Gooda Walker and Feltrim syndicates at Lloyd's in the wake of the Piper Alpha oil rig disaster.

"With rates falling, too much capacity and worrying signs of a developing spiral market, there are parallels with the late 1980s as more capital piles in regardless," Charles Harbord-Hammond, managing director of CBSL, said in a market report.

"There is no doubt that mini-spirals are beginning to be built up. As pressure on income increases through 1997, business will increasingly be written on the back of reinsurance programmes with less and less exclusions," he said.

Gittings said that Lloyd's makes inspection visits to marine excess of loss syndicates to check that underwriters capture and control their aggregate exposures and make assessments to how they would be affected by a series of disasters.
Gittings added that, if necessary, the Lloyd's Regulatory Board would issue directions to specific syndicates limiting their underwriting to prevent a spiral in the market.
